script_blocks:
Scott Amos almost sold it for two hundred dollars on eBay. That was his first instinct, standing in his kitchen with a shrink-wrapped Nintendo cartridge his mother had just handed him from a box in her attic. He'd found it while doing the least glamorous chore imaginable — hauling fifteen years of his own forgotten junk out of her house in Reno, Nevada, because she'd finally had enough of storing it. Instead, less than three months later, that same cartridge sold at auction for nine thousand dollars.

I want to get one number out of the way before anything else, because most retellings of this story get it slightly wrong. Pre-auction estimates floated as high as ten thousand dollars, and that's the figure that ended up in half the headlines. The actual winning bid, including the buyer's premium, was nine thousand dollars. It's a small gap. But if a channel like this one is going to sit here and pick apart other people's factual sloppiness, it should probably get its own numbers straight first.

Here's what actually happened, and here's the part I think is more interesting than the dollar figure itself: nobody in that kitchen had any idea what they were looking at. Not Amos. Not his wife. Not, apparently, his mother, who'd been asking him for over a decade to come get his old stuff and had no clear memory of ever buying him a Nintendo game for Christmas that he never opened. The object itself — thirty-one years old, still sealed in factory plastic, still inside the department-store bag it was carried home in — was, for one afternoon, just clutter on a kitchen counter. Then somebody with the right kind of expertise looked at a photo of it and wrote back within half an hour: "You have an Easter egg."

That phrase is doing a lot of work in this story, and I want to sit with it for a second before we go further, because it tells you something about how this entire market operates. Nobody said "you have money." Nobody said "this is valuable." They said, essentially: you have found a hidden thing inside a system most people never learn exists. And that system — how a piece of shrink-wrapped cardboard from 1988 becomes worth thousands of dollars, who decides that, and whether you should trust them — is really what this video is about. Amos and his Kid Icarus cartridge are the entry point. What's underneath turns out to be a lot stranger, and a lot more contested, than a feel-good local news segment usually lets on.

There's also a strange object at the center of this that's worth naming outright, because it's easy to skip past. What sold for nine thousand dollars was a video game nobody will ever play. That's not incidental — it's the entire point. The moment someone tears that plastic off to actually put the cartridge in a console, the value collapses to whatever a used copy goes for, which is closer to twenty dollars. So what people are really buying, in this hobby, isn't a game at all. It's an untouched moment in time: 1988, a shopping bag, a nine-year-old who never got to open his Christmas present. The plastic wrap is the product. I don't think that's a criticism, exactly. But it's worth being honest about what kind of collecting this actually is before we get further into how it's priced.

Rewind to Mother's Day weekend, 2019. Amos, forty years old by then, finally made the trip his mother had been asking for since he'd moved out — pick up the boxes of his own childhood belongings that had been sitting in her attic for the better part of two decades. Five boxes. Not treasure-hunting, not thrift-store scavenging. Just a grown man doing his mom a favor, expecting nothing more interesting than old yearbooks and a few broken toys.

Four of those five boxes turned out to be exactly what he expected — old yearbooks, a few broken toys, nothing worth a second look. That's not a detail I want to gloss over, because it's easy for a story like this to make "check your attic" sound like decent odds. It isn't. Eighty percent of what Amos hauled out that day was, by his own account, just junk that got thrown away. One of the boxes had a department-store shopping bag inside it. Inside that bag: an unopened copy of Kid Icarus for the Nintendo Entertainment System, still wrapped in its original factory shrink plastic, with the price sticker — thirty-eight dollars and forty-five cents — still attached. Tucked in alongside the cartridge was the actual paper receipt, dated December 8th, 1988. Amos would have been nine years old that Christmas.

Nobody in the family could explain it with any real confidence. Amos remembered the game itself — a neighbor down the street had owned a copy, and by his own account he "was never that good of a gamer guy" at it. But he had no memory of receiving this specific one. His mother's best theory, offered decades later, was that she must have bought it as a Christmas gift, tucked it away somewhere for safekeeping closer to the holiday, and then simply lost track of where she'd put it. Whatever the real explanation is, it isn't fully recoverable at this distance, and I'm not going to pretend it is. Memory doesn't come with a receipt the way this cartridge did — which is, as it turns out, the entire reason this find became valuable at all.

Amos's first instinct was the ordinary one: he figured it might fetch "a couple hundred dollars" on eBay, and he left it sitting on the kitchen counter while he thought it over. It was his own casual move to ask around — reaching out to a couple of people he knew who followed vintage game collecting — that changed the direction of the whole story. One of them replied within half an hour. That's the message that got the cartridge off the kitchen counter and into a padded shipping box headed for Denver, Colorado, home of a grading company called Wata Games.

Once it arrived, the person on the other end of that process wasn't some anonymous technician. Wata's own CEO, Deniz Kahn, personally told Amos that if the cartridge checked out as authentic, it was, in his words, "something special." That's a company founder taking a personal interest in a random submission from a first-time customer in Nevada — which either means Kahn genuinely gets excited about rare finds, or means a company built on subjective judgment calls has every incentive to make submitters feel like they've stumbled into something extraordinary. I'd guess it's honestly a bit of both, and I don't think those two explanations cancel each other out.

By the time the family understood what they actually had, this had stopped being a private matter. Heritage Auctions put out a press photo of Amos with his wife and two daughters, all smiling around the sealed cartridge like it was a newborn. I don't say that to mock it — genuinely, good for them. I mention it because it's a useful marker of how fast this moved: from "forgotten box in an attic" to "professional press photo distributed by a Dallas auction house" in a matter of weeks.

I don't think this part of the story gets nearly enough attention in the way it's usually retold, and it's worth pausing on. Amos didn't set out to find a rare collectible. He wasn't a collector. He didn't know this market existed. The entire chain of events — attic, to kitchen counter, to grading lab, to auction house — ran through a series of small accidents and one lucky email reply. That's a genuinely different story from the one the headlines implied, where some expert goes hunting and gets rewarded for their knowledge. This is closer to: an object survived, by pure chance, in a form rare enough that when it finally crossed paths with someone who understood what they were looking at, the gap between "junk" and "nine thousand dollars" turned out to be about thirty minutes and one email.

So what actually makes a piece of thirty-one-year-old cardboard worth that kind of money? This is the part most coverage skips entirely, and it's the most interesting part if you care about how the market works rather than just the headline number.

When Amos's cartridge arrived at Wata Games, nobody there particularly cared what was inside the box. That surprised me, researching this: for a factory-sealed game, the cartridge itself is almost irrelevant to the appraisal. What matters is the seal. Nintendo games from this era were shrink-wrapped at the factory in a specific, recognizable pattern — a horizontal seam, sometimes with small vent holes, running across the back of the box. Graders are trained to spot the difference between an untouched factory seal and a reseal: someone who opened a used copy years later and shrink-wrapped it again with a cheap heat gun to pass it off as new. A seal that looks slightly too tight, too loose, or is missing its vent pattern gets rejected outright, no matter how clean the box looks otherwise.

Assuming the seal survives that scrutiny, the grader examines the box itself under strong light, hunting for damage that's basically invisible under normal daylight: crushed corners, a defect collectors call "whitening," where the printed ink has worn thin enough to expose the white cardboard underneath, and any fading from years of sun exposure. Every visible flaw gets weighed against a genuinely unforgiving scale. Wata rates the box on a numeric scale that tops out at ten, and grades the seal separately on a letter scale that tops out at A++. Amos's copy came back an 8.0 for the box and an A for the seal — good, not flawless, but authentic and clean enough to matter to serious buyers.

Here's the detail that actually explains the price, more than the grade itself does: according to Heritage Auctions' own video-game consignment director, there are fewer than ten known sealed copies of Kid Icarus in the hands of collectors anywhere in the world. Not ten good copies — ten, total, in any condition. Compare that to something like Super Mario Bros, which sold roughly forty million copies and was frequently bundled with the console itself, meaning plenty of unopened copies simply never got played and more of them survive today. Kid Icarus was a harder, less iconic game that people were far less likely to leave sealed on a shelf for three decades. Scarcity, not fame, was doing most of the work behind Amos's number. Fame is what does the work in the numbers you're about to hear next — and it does a great deal more of it.

One more thing worth knowing before we get to those numbers: Wata isn't the only company doing this. A rival firm called VGA — Video Game Authority — grades on a completely different hundred-point scale instead of Wata's ten-point-plus-letter system, and newer entrants like CGC and PSA have since built their own scales on top of that. A game graded a "95" by VGA doesn't automatically translate to a specific Wata number; collectors have spent years arguing over rough conversion charts, and a box that would earn a pristine grade from one company can come back "Qualified" — meaning previously opened — from another. For a hobby that runs entirely on trust in a number printed on a label, having several competing labels that don't fully agree with each other is, at minimum, an odd foundation. It's a detail that matters more than it sounds like it should, and we'll see exactly why in a few minutes.

Here's where this stops being about one guy's attic and starts being about an entire market that, in hindsight, was only just getting started the summer Amos found his game. Rewind just two years further, to 2017: the top recorded price anyone had paid for a single sealed video game was thirty thousand dollars, for a high-grade copy of Super Mario Bros. That was, at the time, considered a genuinely startling number for a piece of packaging.

Then, in February 2019 — five months before Amos even opened his mother's boxes — Heritage Auctions ran its first-ever Wata-certified video game sale, becoming the first major auction house to offer graded games at all: a pristine sealed copy of Super Mario Bros went for one hundred thousand, one hundred fifty dollars, more than triple that 2017 record in under two years. It was a headline-making number, a new world record. It's also, and I think this matters, a sale where one of the winning buyers turned out to be Jim Halperin — Heritage Auctions' own co-founder, who was also listed as an advisor to Wata. That relationship wasn't disclosed at the time. We'll come back to that. It's also worth flagging that essentially every record-breaking sale in this story — Amos's included — ran through that same single Dallas auction house. Heritage wasn't just a neutral venue watching a market form around it. It was, and still is, close to the only room this market gets to happen in.

So Amos's nine thousand dollars, arriving five months after that hundred-thousand-dollar sale, wasn't the top of this market. It wasn't close. It was a mid-tier result for a genuinely rare, but not especially famous, title — which, if anything, tells you the market was already real and already large enough to have a clear pecking order. What happened next did not slow down.

In April 2021, a sealed copy of Super Mario Bros — forgotten in a desk drawer since 1986 — sold for six hundred sixty thousand dollars. About three months later, in a single Heritage sale event that ultimately totaled more than eight and a half million dollars across all its lots, a sealed Legend of Zelda sold for eight hundred seventy thousand, and just two days after that, a sealed Super Mario 64 broke a million dollars for the first time in this hobby's history, closing at one million, five hundred sixty thousand. Weeks later, a different sealed Super Mario Bros — one that a fractional-investment platform called Rally had bought for one hundred forty thousand dollars the year before — sold privately for two million dollars, becoming, at that moment, the single most valuable video game ever sold. That record held for five years. This past June, an even earlier and rarer sealed print of the same game — sealed with a glossy sticker instead of shrink wrap, one of only three known copies from its original production run, this time graded not by Wata but by a competing firm called PSA — sold at Heritage for three million dollars.

Lay all of that next to Amos's nine thousand, and the shape of this market becomes obvious. It isn't really about age, or rarity, or nostalgia in the abstract. It's about which handful of titles have become the blue-chip names — Mario, Zelda — that a small circle of extremely wealthy collectors is willing to fight over in public. Kid Icarus is genuinely rarer than any of those Super Mario Bros copies. It will almost certainly never sell for anywhere close to what they do. Rarity sets a floor in this market. Fame sets the ceiling, and the ceiling, it turns out, doesn't have one yet.

I'm not going to pretend that curve of numbers is simply the free market discovering true value, because a fair number of people inside this hobby don't believe that either, and their objections are worth taking seriously. In August 2021 — the same month as that two-million-dollar Super Mario Bros sale — a YouTuber named Karl Jobst published a long investigative video accusing Wata Games and Heritage Auctions of working together to inflate prices: grading games favorably for insiders, allowing employees to buy and sell games they'd personally graded, and not disclosing relationships like the one between Heritage's Jim Halperin and Wata that I mentioned a minute ago. Jobst's video also raised a subtler point that I think is actually the more uncomfortable one: in a hobby this small, where a handful of buyers keep resurfacing in record-breaking sales, an auction house doesn't need to fake a bid to shape the market. It just needs to know, better than anyone bidding against them, exactly who else is in the room.

Those allegations didn't stay online. In May 2022, three named collectors — Jacob Knight, Jack Cribbs, and Jason Dohse, standing in for a class that could reportedly number in the tens of thousands — filed a lawsuit against Wata and its parent company, Collectors Universe, in federal court in California. The complaint accused them of market manipulation, unfair business practices, and — this is the phrase that struck me — "a pattern of racketeering activity." It also spelled out exactly how the money moves, and once you see the incentive structure laid out plainly, the allegations at least make logical sense, whether or not they're ultimately true. Wata's own promotional material reportedly cited an example where grading a single game valued at one million dollars nets the company twenty thousand dollars, a two-percent cut. Heritage, meanwhile, collects roughly twenty percent of a winning bid as buyer's premium, plus another five percent from the seller. Every record-breaking headline is also, quietly, a very good month for both companies — which doesn't prove collusion, but does mean neither company had any financial reason to want these prices to plateau.

The lawsuit also raised a much more mundane complaint that somehow feels more damning than the conspiracy language. Wata had been promising a fifteen-business-day turnaround on grading and routinely taking months — in at least one documented case, over a year and a half. That's not a conspiracy theory. That's a company failing at the basic administrative task its entire business is built on, while simultaneously being accused of quietly steering which games become worth a fortune.

I'll be straightforward about what I don't actually know: I can't tell you with confidence how that lawsuit was ultimately resolved, and I'm not going to pretend otherwise just to give this section a tidy ending. What I can tell you is that the market it accused of manipulation didn't slow down while the case worked its way through the courts. Prices kept climbing for years afterward, right through that three-million-dollar sale this past June. Maybe that means the manipulation claims were overstated. Maybe it means a determined handful of buyers can keep a story going regardless of what any lawsuit concludes. I genuinely don't know which one it is. What I do know is that nearly every headline dollar figure in this story — Amos's nine thousand included — passed at some point through the same small grading industry that a group of its own customers accused, in federal court, of rigging the game.

Which brings us back to a kitchen counter in Reno, and a guy who was never trying to be part of any of this. Amos said, publicly, that he planned to put the money toward a family vacation. Not a portfolio. Not a flip. A trip with his wife and two daughters, funded by a video game his mother apparently bought him at nine years old and then lost track of for thirty-one years. Whatever is happening at the top of this market — the eight-figure private sales, the lawsuits, the grading company its own customers took to federal court — none of it touched Amos's actual experience of the story. He found something. Experts confirmed it was genuine. He sold it for far more than he'd expected, and he took his family on a trip. That's the whole story, at his scale.

I think that's worth sitting with, because it's easy to watch a video like this and walk away with the wrong lesson — that your attic is probably hiding a fortune, or that grading is some kind of shortcut to money. It mostly isn't. The honest lesson is narrower and considerably less exciting: if you find something old, factory-sealed, with its original packaging and any paperwork still attached, don't open it and don't try to clean it up. The seal and the paper trail are most of the value; breaking either one can turn a four-figure item into a five-dollar one overnight. Don't wipe dust off the box with a damp cloth, don't peel off a price sticker to see what's underneath, and don't handle the seal itself more than you have to — oils from bare hands can degrade old plastic faster than you'd expect. Photograph it exactly as it is, from every angle, in good light, and send those photos to an actual grading company or an auction house's consignment department before doing anything else. Given how much the different grading scales can disagree with each other, it's also worth getting more than one opinion before you commit to shipping something off. Amos's copy came with a shopping bag and a dated receipt, and that receipt is specifically what one expert meant by "Easter egg" — not the game itself, but the proof of exactly where it came from and when.

One more distinction worth making, since it cuts the other way: everything above is about finding something already sealed. If you're ever buying a "sealed" vintage game instead of finding one, treat that seal with real suspicion. We already talked about how convincing a reseal can look to an untrained eye, and a cheap heat gun and the right shrink film will fool most people browsing a flea market table. That's exactly the failure mode professional grading exists to catch — which is also exactly why it matters whether the company doing the catching can be trusted in the first place.

Fewer than ten sealed copies of Kid Icarus are known to exist anywhere. One of them spent thirty-one years in an attic in Reno, Nevada, because nobody had a reason to think about it. My guess is that most attics still holding something like that are exactly the ones nobody's gotten around to opening in a long time, either — which is a strange thing to sit with, the next time you're the one being asked to finally clear one out.

_источники.policy: Every core claim tagged VERIFIED / SINGLE SOURCE / DISPUTED / LEGEND. Disputed items are flagged in narration, not asserted.
do_not_claim: Exact location of the attic — most outlets (CNN, Fox News, Digital Trends, MyNintendoNews, DualShockers, TheGamer, GameRant) report Reno, Nevada; one outlet (CNBC) states Humboldt County, California. Script uses Reno, Nevada per majority sourcing and does not assert this as the sole confirmed location.

Final legal resolution of the May 2022 Wata Games / Collectors Universe class-action lawsuit — not asserted as settled, dismissed, or ongoing; script explicitly states the outcome is unknown from available sourcing as of research.
The mother's reason for never giving Amos the game as a child — presented in-script as her own stated theory, not verified fact.
Any claim that Wata or Heritage Auctions engaged in illegal conduct — the lawsuit's allegations are reported as allegations, not established findings.

youtube.description_intro: A sealed Nintendo game sat forgotten in an attic for thirty-one years — then sold at auction for nine thousand dollars. This is the story of how a piece of factory shrink-wrap became worth more than the game inside it, and the multi-million-dollar market (and lawsuit) that grew up around games just like it.
chapters: Why a Sealed Box Beats the Game Inside
youtube.description_notes: Pre-auction estimates for the Kid Icarus cartridge ran as high as $10,000; the actual winning bid, including buyer's premium, was $9,000. The 2022 class-action lawsuit against Wata Games / Collectors Universe is described in this video based on the allegations as filed; its final legal outcome is not confirmed in available sourcing.
